title: Factorise a difference of two squares

say: You give it a difference of two squares, $a^2 - b^2$. It writes it as two **brackets**, $(a - b)(a + b)$.
The key idea: when you multiply those two brackets, the middle terms cancel and only $a^2 - b^2$ is left.

steps.title: Take out the common factor
steps.say: Both terms divide by $2$. Take it out first, so the bracket is a clean difference of squares.

steps.title: Write each as a square
steps.say: $25x^2$ is $(\hl{1}{5x})^2$ and $36$ is $\hl{2}{6}^2$. So the bracket is $a^2 - b^2$ with $a = \hl{1}{5x}$ and $b = \hl{2}{6}$.

steps.title: Write the two brackets
steps.say: $a^2 - b^2$ becomes $(a - b)(a + b)$. Put $\hl{1}{5x}$ and $\hl{2}{6}$ in.

lines.text: Keep the $2$ at the front. It is part of the answer.

say: You give it two brackets multiplied together, like $(2x + 3)(x - 4)$. It gives back one expression with no brackets, with like terms collected.
The key idea: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second. Two terms by two terms makes four products.

steps.title: Multiply by the first term
steps.say: Take the first bracket one term at a time. Multiply the whole second bracket by $3x$, then by $-2$.

steps.title: Remove the brackets
steps.say: Multiply each term inside. Watch the signs: $-2$ times $+5$ is $-10$.

steps.title: Collect like terms
steps.say: The two $x$ terms are like terms. Add them: $15x - 4x = \hl{1}{11x}$.

say: You give it two expressions with $x^2$, $x$ and number terms, joined by a plus or minus. It gives back one simplified expression.
The key idea: only like terms combine. $x^2$ goes with $x^2$, $x$ with $x$, numbers with numbers. A minus in front of a bracket flips every sign inside it.

steps.title: Remove the brackets
steps.say: The minus sign in front of the second bracket flips every sign inside it. Change them one by one.

steps.title: Group like terms
steps.say: Put the $x^2$ terms together, the $x$ terms together, and the numbers together.

steps.title: Add each group
steps.say: Add inside each bracket.

say: You give it an expression with four terms, like $ax + ay + bx + by$. It writes it as a product of two **brackets**.
The key idea: pair the terms so each pair has a common factor. Both pairs then leave the same bracket, and that bracket comes out.

steps.title: Group in pairs
steps.say: Put the first two terms in one bracket and the last two in another. Keep the sign in front of each term.

steps.title: Take out each common factor
steps.say: Take the common factor out of each pair. Choose the second one so it leaves the **same** bracket as the first.

lines.text: In the second pair the factor is $-2$, not $2$. That is what makes $-4y - 6$ become $-2(2y+3)$.

steps.title: Take out the common bracket
steps.say: The bracket $\hl{1}{(2y + 3)}$ is common to both parts. Take it out. What is left forms the second bracket.

lines.text: Check by multiplying out: you get $6xy + 9x - 4y - 6$ back.

say: You give it a formula and the letter you want as the subject. It gives you that letter on its own, equal to an expression in the others.
The key idea: do the same thing to both sides, one move at a time. If the letter appears twice, gather it onto one side and **factorise** it out.

example.question: Make $q$ the subject of the formula $m = \dfrac{2q + 5}{q - 3}$.

steps.title: Clear the fraction
steps.say: Multiply both sides by $q - 3$ to remove the fraction. Then multiply out the bracket.

steps.title: Gather the q terms
steps.say: $\hl{1}{q}$ is on both sides. Move every term with $\hl{1}{q}$ to the left and every other term to the right.

steps.title: Factorise out q
steps.say: Take $\hl{1}{q}$ out as a common factor, so it appears only once.

steps.title: Divide to isolate q
steps.say: Divide both sides by $m - 2$.

say: You give it a bracket raised to a power, $(a + b)^n$. It writes it out as a sum of $n + 1$ terms.
The key idea: each term is a **binomial coefficient** times a power of $a$ times a power of $b$. The power of $a$ goes down by one as the power of $b$ goes up by one.

steps.title: Find the coefficients
steps.say: The coefficients are the numbers $\binom{4}{r}$ for $r = 0$ to $4$.

lines.text: The row is symmetric, so $\binom{4}{3} = 4$ and $\binom{4}{4} = 1$.

steps.title: Write out the five terms
steps.say: Take $a = 2x$ and $b = -3$. In each term the power of $2x$ goes down and the power of $-3$ goes up. The two powers always add to $4$.

lines.text: Put the $-3$ in brackets. The sign is raised to the power too.

steps.title: Work out each term
steps.say: Evaluate the powers, then multiply each term out.

title: Find a given term/coefficient of a binomial expansion

say: You give it a bracket $(a + b)^n$ and the power you want. It gives the one term, or its coefficient, without expanding the rest.
The key idea: the general term is $T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r}a^{n-r}b^r$. Match the power you want to find $r$.

example.question: Find the coefficient of $x^4$ in the expansion of $(3x - 2)^6$.

steps.title: Write the general term
steps.say: Take $a = 3x$ and $b = -2$. The general term has $\hl{1}{r}$ as the power of $b$.

steps.title: Find r
steps.say: The power of $x$ in this term is $6 - \hl{1}{r}$. Set it equal to $4$ and solve.

steps.title: Substitute r
steps.say: Put $r = 2$ into the general term. Evaluate the coefficient and the power of $-2$.

lines.text: The question asks for the **coefficient**: the number in front of $x^4$.

say: You give it two polynomials. It gives back one **expanded** polynomial with no brackets.
The key idea: every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second, then you collect like terms.

steps.title: Multiply each term across
steps.say: Take each term of the first bracket and multiply it by the whole second bracket. Here $\hl{1}{2x}$ and $\hl{2}{1}$ each go through $x^2-3x+5$.

steps.title: Open the brackets
steps.say: Multiply every term inside. Take care with the signs.

steps.title: Collect like terms
steps.say: Add the $x^2$ terms together and the $x$ terms together.

lines.text: Check one value: at $x=1$ both forms give $9$.

title: Factorise a sum/difference of two cubes

say: You give it an expression of the form $a^3 \pm b^3$. It gives back a product of a **linear** bracket and a **quadratic** bracket.
The key idea: both terms are perfect cubes, so a fixed pattern factorises them. Only the signs differ between the sum and the difference.

steps.title: Write both as cubes
steps.say: Check that each term is a perfect cube. $27x^3 = (3x)^3$ and $8 = 2^3$, so $\hl{1}{a=3x}$ and $\hl{2}{b=2}$.

steps.title: Use the pattern
steps.say: For a difference of cubes, the bracket keeps the minus sign and the quadratic has plus signs.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.say: Put $a=3x$ and $b=2$ into the pattern.

steps.title: Simplify the quadratic
steps.say: Work out each term in the second bracket.

lines.text: Check by multiplying out: you get $27x^3 - 8$ back.

say: You give it an expression with surds and brackets, like $(\sqrt{x}+1)(\sqrt{x}-1)$. It gives back a **simplified** form.
The key idea: multiply out the brackets as usual, then use $\sqrt{x}\times\sqrt{x} = x$ to remove the surds that cancel.

steps.title: Multiply out the brackets
steps.say: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second. One product is $\sqrt{x}\times\sqrt{x}$.

steps.title: Remove the square root pair
steps.say: A square root times itself gives what is inside: $\hl{1}{\sqrt{x}\sqrt{x}} = \hl{1}{x}$.

steps.title: Collect like terms
steps.say: The two $\sqrt{x}$ terms are like terms. Add them.

say: You give it two fractions with $x$ in the denominators. It gives back **one** fraction.
The key idea: fractions only add when the denominators match, so multiply top and bottom of each by what the other denominator has.

steps.title: Find a common denominator
steps.say: The denominators are different, so multiply them together. Top and bottom of the first fraction get $\hl{1}{(x-1)}$. Top and bottom of the second get $\hl{2}{(x+2)}$.

steps.title: Add the numerators
steps.say: The denominators now match. Write one fraction with one denominator.

steps.title: Simplify the top
steps.say: Open the brackets in the numerator, then collect like terms. Leave the denominator as it is.

title: Divide a polynomial by a linear or quadratic

say: You give it a polynomial and a linear divisor. It gives back the **quotient**, and the remainder if there is one.
The key idea: divide the first term of what is left by the first term of the divisor, multiply back, subtract, and repeat until the degree drops below the divisor's.

steps.title: Divide the first terms
steps.say: Divide the first term, $2x^3$, by the first term of the divisor, $x$. That gives the first term of the quotient. Multiply it back and subtract.

steps.title: Repeat on what is left
steps.say: Do the same with $3x^2 - 11x + 6$. The first term $3x^2$ divided by $x$ is the next term of the quotient.

steps.title: Finish the division
steps.say: One more round. If the remainder is $0$, then $(x-3)$ is a factor.

lines.text: The remainder is $0$, so the quotient is $2x^2 + 3x - 2$.

steps.say: Write $f(x)$ as a product. Then factorise the quadratic and set each bracket to $0$.
